newsitem.title: USA: Korean peace talks meeting to resume Friday.
newsitem.headline: Korean peace talks meeting to resume Friday.

text.p: Negotiators for the United States and the two Koreas were to resume discussions on Friday aimed at winning Pyongyang's unqualified agreement to enter into landmark peace talks with its arch-rival, Seoul.
The three teams held an inconclusive meeting on Wednesday in New York but all sides reported progress and said they hoped to settle the issue on Friday, also in New York.

The meeting was called to hear Pyongyang's formal response to a year-old U.S.-South Korean proposal for four-party peace talks, in which China would also participate, that would finally close the books on the 1950-53 Korean War by replacing the fraying armistice with a peace treaty.

North Korea began Wednesday's crucial meeting by essentially accepting the peace talks proposal but then tied that acceptance to a new demand for international assistance to meet severe food shortages, U.S. officials told Reuters.

Despite these demands, no new food aid pledges -- either from Washington or Seoul -- were expected before North Korea responds conclusively to a proposal for Korean peninsula peace talks, U.S. officials said.

U.S. officials have said Pyongyang cannot expect a massive effort to deal with its food problems until it enters peace talks and begins to defuse tensions on the volatile and heavily armed Korean peninsula.

One senior official said the United States worked hard to avoid being put in a position where food aid was seen as a reward for North Korea's acceptance of the peace talks proposal. Washington speeded up normal bureaucratic procedures to announce an extra $15 million in assistance last Monday.
Asked if he expected the United States or South Korea to announce additional food aid before talks resume on Friday, the official said: "No, I don't."

"My expectation is that sooner or later the North Koreans are going to feel they accomplished their first priority: They sensitized the outside world to their needs ... and they will turn to the question of peace talks and give a response. I'm still expecting that response will be favorable," he said.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns confirmed that Washington planned no new food aid commitments at this time. "I think the United States has done what it can," he said.
Nevertheless, when discussions resume on Friday, Burns said, "we hope that at the end of the day we'll be able to say North Korea agrees to four-party talks."
After some skepticism in Washington and elsewhere, it has been widely accepted that impoverished Stalinist North Korea is facing serious food shortages bordering on famine.

North Korea and independent experts say the country needs 2.3 million tons of food this year. Pyongyang claims it can scrape together about half that amount, with the rest coming from international donors. Some U.S. analysts doubt this.
The U.N. World Food Program recently appealed for 200,000 metric tons of food, with Washington offering one-quarter.
Humanitarian activists on Thursday pressed Japan to donate some of its rice hoard to North Korea and urged the United States to work with China to speed delivery of food aid.
